paragraphs: On Thursday, Mia gave a talk to the Explorers in the school library. The title of her talk was "Music in Nature." She stood in front of a big picture of a forest. Her science textbook was open on the table. Leo sat in the front row, and May sat next to him. Mia had a small card with her notes, but her voice was clear. "Many animals make music," she said. "Today I will give you three examples."

"My first example is birds," said Mia. "Birds sing early in the morning." She played a short bird song on a small speaker. It was a bright and high song. Leo tried to sing like the bird, and Teacher Kim smiled. "A single bird can sing for ten minutes." "My textbook says that a bird sings to show its tree to other birds." "Some birds also sing together, for example in a crowded tree." Lily wrote the word "example" in her notebook.

"My second example is frogs," said Mia. "A frog can sit on a leaf, and it can sing very loudly." She showed a photo of a small pale green frog. The frog had big eyes and a soft body. "After rain, many frogs sing at night," she said. "Some people say that the frogs celebrate the rain." "Is that a fact?" asked May. "No, it is only an idea," said Mia, "but it is a nice idea."

"My third example is insects," said Mia. "Insects such as bees and flies make a soft buzz." "Bees fly from flower to flower, and each bee makes a small sound." "A hundred bees make a loud buzz together." "Among the trees, many insects make sounds at the same time." "The forest at night is like a big band," said Leo. "Yes!" said Mia. "It sounds like jazz, because every player makes a different sound."

Then Teacher Kim asked, "Is there music at our school?" Everybody stopped and listened. They heard a loud sound from the trees outside. "It is an insect, and it sings all day!" said Mia. Leo laughed and said, "Our school has a jazz band too." "Mia, your talk was great," said May. "Can I give a talk next week?" "Yes," said Teacher Kim. "Choose a topic, and give two examples." Lily wrote a title for the blog: "Music in Nature."

sentences.text: On Thursday, Mia gave a talk to the Explorers in the school library.

Her science textbook was open on the table.
Leo sat in the front row, and May sat next to him.
Mia had a small card with her notes, but her voice was clear.
"Many animals make music," she said.
"Today I will give you three examples."
"My first example is birds," said Mia.
"Birds sing early in the morning."
She played a short bird song on a small speaker.
It was a bright and high song.
Leo tried to sing like the bird, and Teacher Kim smiled.

"Some birds also sing together, for example in a crowded tree."

"My second example is frogs," said Mia.

"After rain, many frogs sing at night," she said.
"Some people say that the frogs celebrate the rain."
"Is that a fact?" asked May.
"No, it is only an idea," said Mia, "but it is a nice idea."
"My third example is insects," said Mia.
"Insects such as bees and flies make a soft buzz."
"Bees fly from flower to flower, and each bee makes a small sound."

"Among the trees, many insects make sounds at the same time."
"The forest at night is like a big band," said Leo.
"Yes!" said Mia.
"It sounds like jazz, because every player makes a different sound."
Then Teacher Kim asked, "Is there music at our school?"
Everybody stopped and listened.
They heard a loud sound from the trees outside.
"It is an insect, and it sings all day!" said Mia.
